INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Teachers Unify to End Gun Violence (Teachers Unify) is a national grassroots movement of educators, school staff, and allies working at the
intersection of education and gun violence prevention
to advocate for safe school communities. By amplifying the voices of those on the front lines of this public
health crisis, Teachers Unify empowers school communities to demand a seat at the table where local,
state, and national safety decisions are made. It also
supports teachers and staff navigating the fear and
impact of gun violence through prevention, intervention, and in the aftermath of a tragedy.
The National Association of School Nurses
(NASN) is a nonprofit specialty nursing organization,
organized in 1968 and incorporated in 1977, representing school nurses. NASN has nearly 20,000 members and 51 affiliates representing 50 states and the
Overseas School Health Nurses Association. NASN
equips s chool nurses with evidence- based resources
and support to be leaders in school health, and empowers school nurses to promote student health,
safety, and academic achievement through advocacy,
education, research, and community connections.
The National Association of School Psychologists (NASP) is a professional association representing more than 24,000 school psychologists,

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in

2
graduate students, and related professionals throughout the United States and around the world. As the
world’s largest organization of school psychologists,
NASP works to advance effective practices to improve
students’ learning, behavior, and mental health.
NASP’s vision is that all children and youth should be
able to thrive in school, at home, and throughout life.
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF
ARGUMENT
School gun violence is an appalling scourge in the
United States, and it is often carried out with assault
weapons, including in particular the AR -15 semi-automatic rifle and its variants with enhanced militarystyle features and magazine capacities. But the havoc
that assault weapons wreak is not limited to the violence itself, as awful as that toll is. One of our society’s
main responses to school gun violence has been to institute an array of active shooter drills, which are now
pervasive in the nation’s  school systems. And research is making it increasingly apparent that active
shooter drills, though meant to foster school safety,
further undermin e American schoolchildren’s basic
sense of security and well -being. Assault weapons
thus do not merely kill and maim our nation’s children and their teachers with numbing regularity —
but one of the chief responses to the mayhem they inflict diminishes the psychological and emotional
health of American youth even further by imposing on
them yet another layer of trauma and anxiety.
I.A. Gun violence has reached epidemic proportions in the United States, especially for children. Although most gun deaths do not occur in schools, gun

3
violence in schools is itself an extraordinary public
health concern. There have been hundreds of school
shootings in this country since the killings at Columbine High School in Littlet on, Colorado in 1999, and
school shootings are now a thoroughly ingrained part
of American life. In school shootings (as in other mass
shootings), assault weapons are often the weapon of
choice because of the tremendous carnage they can inflict in a short period of time. It is no coincidence that
the perpetrators at Sandy Hook Elementary School in
Newtown, Connecticut, Marjor y Stoneman Douglas
High School in Parkland, Florida, and Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, among many other
school shootings, all used variants of the AR-15 rifle.
B. A predominant response to school shootings in
school systems throughout the country has been to institute active shooter drills. M ore than 95% of U.S.
public schools now regularly conduct such drills. Indeed, in a majority of states, active shooter drills are
mandated by state law.  Active shooter drills are not
only pervasive, they are also big business , with forprofit companies charg ing school districts for trainings.
C. Research is increasingly showing, however,
that active shooter drills, though intended to promote
school safety, in fact can aggravate the already tragic
effects of gun violence in schools by adding a new
layer of trauma and anxiety resulting from the drills
themselves. Especially depending on how they are
conducted, active shooter drills can cause children to
picture themselves in life- threatening circumstances
and can also heighten the impression that an actual
active shooter event is likely to occur. In surveys,

4
young children and teenagers acknowledge the adverse impact of active shooter drills on their sense of
well-being, and school officials likewise point out that
students often feel less safe after a drill than before.
II.A. The first-hand accounts of teachers, school
nurses, and school psychologists illustrate the ill effects of active shooter drills. Teachers are at the front
lines of school safety. Teachers are typically willing to
put their own lives at risk to protect the lives of
youngsters in their care, and, indeed, teachers were
among those killed at Columbine, Sandy Hook, Marjory Stoneman Douglas, and Uvalde, among many
other similar tragedies. Although with younger children care is often taken to mask the true intent of the
drills, teachers see with their own eyes that active
shooter drills can cause students to imagine themselves amidst an actual school shooting,  while at the
same time further desensitizing them to the reality
that deadly school shootings have become commonplace in this country.
B. School- based health professionals , including
school nurses and school psychologists, also play a vital role in support ing the well-being of students and
staff during and after active shooter drills. L ike the
experiences of teachers, the first-hand experiences of
school nurses and school psychologists underscore
what underlying research increasingly reveals: Gun
violence in schools, frequently effectuated with assault weapons, inflicts damage on our country not just
via the violence itself, but also because active shooter
drilling, imposed in  response to the violence, independently harms American schoolchildren by undermining even further their sense of safety and security.

5
Of course, school active shooter drilling reflects just
one way that assault weapons have transformed facets of American life, like basic school safety, that previously we took for granted.
ARGUMENT
I. Gun V iolence In A merican Schools Is A
Grievous P roblem And Has Spawned
Ubiquitous Active Shooter Drills
Exacerbating Schoolchildren’s Trauma.
A. Firearms violence in schools, often
perpetrated with assault weapons, is a
serious and growing phenomenon.
Gun violence in general is a grave public health
issue in the United States, including for children.
“Each year, more than 100,000 individuals in the
United States, including more than 17,000 children,
are shot directly with firearms. Indeed, firearms are
now the leading cause of death among children and
teens in the United States.” National Academies of
Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, School Active
Shooter Drills: Mitigating Risks to Mental, Emotional, and Behavioral Health  26 (Nat’l Acads. Press
2025), https://tinyurl.com/4xu8w6uh.
Although most gun deaths do not occur in schools,
gun violence in schools is itself a serious and growing
problem. “While accounting for a small portion of annual gun violence deaths, school shootings are an increasingly frightening reality in the United States.”
Jeff R. Temple, Elizabeth Baumler & Christian Page

6
Owen, Drills or Distress? Understanding the Psychological Effects of Active Shooter Drills on Adolescents,
42 J. Sch. Nursing 521, 521 (2025). Indeed, “[o]ver the
past several years, firearm violence in K –12 schools
has increased.” National Academies , supra, at 26.
“[N]early 400,000 students have been exposed to gun
violence (specifically in K –12 schools) since the Columbine mass shooting that took place in Littleton ,
Colorado, in 1999. Notable upticks in school- based
firearm violence have been documented s ince 2015.”
Id. at 26-27 (citation omitted).
There have been hundreds of school shootings in
the United States since 1999, and school shootings are
now such an ingrained part of American life that several of them have been etched into our national consciousness. “The shooting at Columbine High School
occurred on April 20, 1999.” Id. at 30. Twelve students
and a teacher were killed (in addition to the two student shooters, who died by suicide), and 20 others
were injured. “At the time, it was the deadliest mass
shooting at a K–12 school in U.S. history. This tragic
event remains one of the most infamous school shootings in the United States and is often mentioned when
a new school shooting occurs.” Id.
“On December 14, 2012, the deadliest school
shooting at an elementary school in U.S. history occurred at Sandy Hook Elementary School” in Newtown, Connecticut. Id.  at 34. The shooter killed 20
first-grade children (ages six and seven) and six staff
members, including teachers, the principal, and the
school psychologist.

7
“On February 14, 2018, a shooting at Marjory
Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida,
resulted in 17 deaths —the deadliest school shooting
at a high school to date.” Id. Those who lost their lives
include 14 students and three teachers, and another
17 victims were wounded. Id.
And “[o]n May 24, 2022, a shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, resulted in the
deaths of 19 students and two teachers,” and injuries
to 18 others. Id. at 35. This was “the second-deadliest
K-12 school shooting recorded in the U.S., trailing
only the 2012 attack at Sandy Hook Elementary in
Connecticut that left 26 victims dead.” Vanessa Romo,
Texas Community Struggles with Second -Deadliest
School Shooting in U.S. History, NPR (May 25, 2022),
https://perma.cc/4NJC-JQLV.
In school shootings (as in other mass shootings),
assault weapons are often the weapon of choice because of the ease with which they can be employed to
kill and inflict devastating injuries on many people in
a short burst of time. The Sandy Hook shooter used a
Bushmaster XM15-E2S semi-automatic rifle, which is
an AR15- type assault weapon. CNN, Sandy Hook
School Shootings Fast Facts  (Oct. 2, 2026), https://tinyurl.com/4uybsb7z. In the Marjory Stoneman Douglas shooting, the assailant deployed a semi-automatic
Smith & Wesson M&P 15, which is also an AR15-type
assault weapon. Bart Jansen, Florida Shooting Suspect Bought Gun Legally, Authorities Say, USA Today
(Feb. 15, 2018), https://tinyurl.com/3rxzf8kw. And the
Uvalde gunman armed himself with a Daniel Defense
M4 V7 semi-automatic rifle, which, again, is an AR15-

8
type assault weapon. Briana Koeneman, Manufacturer of Gun Used in Uvalde Shooting Facing Backlash, Scripps News ( May 31, 2022) ,
https://tinyurl.com/4txzzudy. The Uvalde perpetrator
had also brought with him a Smith & Wesson M&P
15 but left that weapon behind in his vehicle outside
the school. Jeremy Rogalski & Tina Macías, Search
Warrants Reveal How Much Firepower Uvalde Shooting Suspect Had i n Mass Shooting , KHOU 11 ( June
2, 2022) , https://tinyurl.com/3jxwx84y. See Conn.
Resp. Br. 30-31; Cook Cnty. Resp. Br. 44-45.
B. A prominent reaction has been to
mandate active shooter drills, which are
pervasive and often required by state
law.
Our society’s reaction to the continuing spate of
school shootings has largely been one of response rather than prevention. One of the most common reactions in jurisdictions throughout the country has been
to institute a range of active shooter drills.
“The term active shooter drills has been used to describe a range of practices including but not limited to
lockdown drills, options-based drills, and full-scale simulation exercises.” National Academies, supra, at 1; see
NASP, Guidance for School Safety and Lockdown
Drills, https://tinyurl.com/2pcxdprj (last visited Oct.
27, 2026) . “ U.S. federal agencies define an active
shooter as ‘an individual actively engaged in killing or
attempting to kill people in a confined and populated
area’ with a firearm.” Nat ional Academies, supra, at
39. “The FBI expands this definition to include more
than one individual in an incident and omits the word

9
‘confined’ because the term excludes incidents that occur outside buildings. Active shooter events can take
place in many different locations, including schools,
movie theaters, and workplaces.” Id.
“[S]chool active shooter drills have become one of
the most commonly implemented safety practices”  in
response to school shootings. National Academies, supra, at 27. “ Given the reality of school shootings …
lockdown or active shooter drills are likely a fact of life
in the United States” for the foreseeable future. Temple, supra, 42 J. Sch. Nursing at 522.
Active shooter drills have become a pervasive feature of American schools. “Since the 1999 Columbine
shooting, active shooter drills have proliferated in
America’s school systems at an exponential rate.”
Everytown for Gun Safety Support Fund, The Impact
of Active Shooter Drills in Schools  (updated May 14,
2024), https://tinyurl.com/nhkaa9y6. “ Today, more
than 25 years after Columbine, 95% of U.S. public
schools conduct active shooter drills as part of emergency response training.” National Academies, supra,
at 1. See Pauline Moore, Melisssa Kay Dil iberti &
Brian A. Jackson, Are Active Shooter Drills in K –12
Schools Aligned with Best Practices? Insights from Recent Surveys of Educators 4, RAND ( Sep. 24, 2025) ,
https://tinyurl.com/fekdnp8s (“active shooter drills  ...
have become nearly universal in K –12 schools across
the country” (emphasis omitted)).
In a substantial majority of states, active shooter
drills are required by state law. “The number of school
active shooter events has been increasing since the
early 2000s. While these events remain statistically

10
rare, they have a profound impact on communities and
school systems. A number of state legislatures have responded by mandating the implementation of active
shooter drills in schools to prepare for the possibility of
an active shooter event.” National Academies, supra,
at 75.
“[A]s of early 2024, at least 37 states required K–
12 schools to conduct school active shooter –related
drills, typically on an annual basis.” Id. “[V]ariation in
state requirements for active shooter drills … range
from zero to four or more mandated drills per year .”
Id. at 112. “Although 13 states do not have mandates
for such drills, school districts in these states may conduct them voluntarily.” Id. at 75. “Given the growing
fear regarding school shooting incidents, active
shooter drills are likely to become,” if anything, an
even “more common and routine component of the K-
12 institutional structure.” N’dea Moore- Petinak et
al., Active Shooter Drills in the United States: A National Study of Youth Experiences and Perceptions, 67
J. Adolescent Health  509, 510 ( 2020), https://tinyurl.com/3ksy28pd.
Active shooter drills are also big business. “[F]orprofit companies charg[e] school districts … for trainings,” and “the active shooter drill industry is part of
a school safety industry worth” billions of dollars.
Everytown for Gun Safety Support Fund, supra;
Shaila Dewan & D ana Goldstein, What Keeps Students Safe in School? Prevention, Not Defenses, Experts Say , N.Y. Times ( Oct. 16, 2026) ,
https://tinyurl.com/ye26ysu5 (“[M]easures schools are
using to shield students from an armed attac k [are]

11
fueling what market research firms say is a $4 billion
school safety industry.”).2
C. Active shooter drills can be traumatic
and add to a culture of fear.
There is a growing realization that active shooter
drills, though intended to enhance school safety, in
fact compound the already tragic effects of gun violence in schools by adding a new layer of stress and
trauma resulting from the drills themselves. “[W]hile
school violence is statistically rare, it can have lasting
psychological effects on students and staff.” National
Academies, supra, at 19. “ [R]ecent studies indicate
that,” over and above the impact of actual violence,
“school active shooter drills—designed to prepare students for such incidents —may also exacerbate anxiety, fear, and stress.” Id.3

2 Active shooter drills are not our society’s only response to
school shootings; some parents are now outfitting their children
with bulletproof backpacks, although as one parent noted, “I
know it won’t hold up against an AR -15.” Coralie Kraft, When
Back-to-School Shopping Includes Bulletproof Backpacks , N.Y.
Times Mag. (Sep. 21, 2026), https://tinyurl.com/y4khtvzj.
3 The American Psychological Association defines trauma as
“any disturbing experience that results in significant fear, helplessness, dissociation, confusion, or other disruptive feelings intense enough to have a long -lasting negative effect .” Trauma,
American Psychological Association Dictionary of Psychology,
https://tinyurl.com/3f9ve5ze (last visited Oct. 2, 2026); see also
U.S. Dep’t of Health & Human Servs., Substance Abuse and
Mental Health Servs. Admin., SAM HSA’s Concept of Trauma
and Guidance for a Trauma -Informed Approach  (2014),

12
“[S]chool active shooter events are dynamically
different from all other emergency threats,” and
school active shooter drills can  “have mental, emotional, and behavioral health effects that are distinctly different from those associated with other
safety drills.” Id. at 41. Though the specific contours
of a school active shooter drill may vary depending on
the age of the students, these drills “differ from other
measures intended to curb school gun violence” insofar as “they require students to actively engage in an
imagined violent scenario.” Cassandra C. Howard et
al., Districts Implementation of Active Shooter Drill
Policies, 33 Crim. Just. Pol’y Rev. 667, 670 (2022).
Accordingly, active shooter drills “may have unintended and negative mental health consequences on
students.” Temple, supra, 42 J. Sch. Nursing  at 523.
Active shooter drills “may cause students to imagine
themselves in a life-threatening school shooting event
or may create an impression that an active shooter
event is likely to occur.” National Academies , supra,
at 148. “[D]rilling” can “serve[] to highlight perceived
vulnerabilities by the students, leading them to express feeling significantly less safe at school” after the
drilling than before. Jaclyn Schildkraut, Amanda B.
Nickerson & Thomas Ristoff et al., Locks, Lights, Out

https://tinyurl.com/rb2vnpcj (similar). Common reactions to active shooter drills in schools—including fear, anxiety, and an undermined sense of safety  and well-being—fall well within this
framework.

13
of Sight: Assessing Students’ Perceptions of Emergency Preparedness Across Multiple Lockdown Drills,
19 J. Sch. Violence 93, 102 (2020).
Indeed, in surveys, “large number[s] of youths …
noted the negative impact of [active shooter] drills on
their emotional well-being.” Moore-Petinak, supra, 67
J. Adolescent Health at 512. “Nearly a third of principals and teachers reported being aware of students
experiencing trauma or heightened anxiety after
drills.” Moore, supra; see Michael G. Huskey & Nadine M. Connell, Preparation or Provocation? Student
Perceptions of Active Shooter Drills , 32 Crim. Just.
Pol’y Rev. 3, 15-17 (2021) (high school study  finding
that “experiencing an active shooter drill” was associated with significant increases in student fear, “ increased perceptions of risk, and a decrease in
perceptions of school safety”).
Research focused on schoolchildren’s and teachers’ social media indicated that active shooter drills
are followed by social media posts showing a 39% increase in words associated with depression, a 42% increase in words associated with stress and anxiety,
and a 23% increase in words associated with physiological health problems (e.g., blood, pain, clinics, and
pills). National Academies, supra, at 157. “Likewise ,
words associated with concerns about death increased
22% following active shooter drills.” Id.  at 157- 58.
“Teachers who participated in the study recalled students ‘texting their parents, praying, crying’ because
they felt like ‘they were going to die’ during” an active
shooter drill.  Caroline Bologna, The Mental Health
Toll of Active Shooter Drills in Schools, HuffPost (May
25, 2022), https://tinyurl.com/4nah9bd9. “Other post-

14
drill trends included increases in expressions of social
and personal concerns, fewer positive statements,
more requests for help, and increased profanity.
These trends were sustained throughout the 90- day
post-drill period, suggesting that the negative impacts of active shooter drills are not fleeting but last
at least 3 months.” National Academies , supra, at
157. “[A]ll school levels (elementary, middle, and high
school) demonstrated negative post- drill effects.” Id.;
see Everytown for Gun Safety Support Fund, supra
(also discussing underlying research).
The trauma that can result from active shooter
drills is especially severe when the drills consist of
live simulations. NASP et al., Best Practice Guidance
for School Safety and Lockdown Drills: Preparing for
Active Threats 7 (Apr. 2026)  (“NASP”), https://tinyurl.com/82h5ckwc. Live simulations are exercises
that mimic active shooter events and can include
some or all of the following components:
• The activation of emergency alarms.
• The presence of an individual pretending to
be an active shooter or law enforcement officer, or both, inside a school.
• The firing of a gun with blanks.
• Recordings of the sound of a gun being
fired.
• Simulated injury or violence.
• An attempt by an intruder to breach classroom doors inside a school.

15
• The expectation that individuals inside the
school will role play fighting an intruder.
National Academies, supra, at 36.
Live simulation drills are sometimes conducted
without any advance notice to students or parents, or
even teachers, further aggravating the trauma that
children may experience. “Active shooter drills at a
school may be publicly preannounced or may occur
without being announced to staff, families, students ,
and community stakeholders.” Id. at 80-81; see Moore,
supra. These exercises “may incorporate such components as real or simulated gunshot sounds, guns with
blank ammunition, pellet guns, fake text messag es,
theatrical makeup with fake blood, informed actor
volunteers, and individuals pretending to be an active
shooter roaming the halls and attempting to open
classroom doors; such simulations have sometimes
been carried out with students.” National Academies,
supra, at 47. “In some cases, drills may simulate a
real emergency by incorporating deceptive strategies,
such as falsely announcing a real emergency or having a law enforcement officer enter the school as if
they were an active shooter.” Id. at 306.4

4 Even when live simulation drills do not involve students,
they may still cause trauma. NASP, supra , at 7. In particular,
more than 100,000 U.S. schoolteachers are veterans, and the
chaotic sights and sounds associated with live-simulation active
shooter drills can be triggering for that population. See Nat’l Ctr.
Educ. Stats., Digest of Education Statistics  (2022), https://tinyurl.com/2yu4yr8k; Evie Blad & Madeline Will, “I Felt More
Traumatized Than Trained”: Active-Shooter Drills Take Toll on

16
II. The Trauma Resulting From Active Shooter
Drills Is Reflected In The Experience Of
Teachers, School Nurses, And School
Psychologists.
A. The experience of teachers illustrates
the ill effects of active shooter drills on
our nation’s schoolchildren.
Teachers are on the front line s of school safety.
Students, especially younger children, often depend
on their teachers for guidance and comfort during an
active shooter drill, whether the teacher’s instruction
is “be quiet and don’t make a sound,” “hide under your
desks and don’t move,” “wait until a uniformed police
officer comes to get us,” and/or “everything is going to
be alright.” Many teachers report that, if the moment
were to come, they would lay down their lives to protect the well-being of children and youth in their care.
As noted, teachers were among the fatalities at Columbine, Sandy Hook, Marjory Stoneman Douglas ,
and Uvalde, as well as many other school shootings.
Abbey Clements is a long-time elementary school
teacher, a Sandy Hook survivor, and a co -founder of
Teachers Unify to End Gun Violence. On December
14, 2012, she was teaching her second -grade class at
Sandy Hook Elementary School when the shooter entered the school with an assault weapon and embarked on his killing spree. Ms. Clements huddled in

When asked if Sandy Hook Elementary School responded to the tragedy by instituting a program of active shooter drills, Ms. Clements explains that the
answer is no. Responsible Sandy Hook officials understood that active shooter drilling would be traumatic
for children, families, and staff, and ind eed would be
especially traumatic at a school that had already undergone an actual, and deadly, shooting (and even
more so with respect to an elementary school , where
the children are so young). The validity of this assessment is reflected in research studies showing that the
deleterious effects of active shooter drills are heightened for individuals and communities that have already been victimized by violence, including and
especially school violence. See, e.g., National Academies, supra, at 223- 24 (“ School communities that
have experienced mass violence also have a significantly greater presence and persistence of PTSD .”);
NASP, supra, at 8 (“[I]f a child, group of children, or
school community has experienced tra uma due to
school violence, alternative teaching and training
may be necessary to avoid further trauma exposure.”).
The events of December 14, 2012, were uniquely
horrific for Ms. Clements, her students, and the
Sandy Hook community. They ultimately altered the
trajectory of Ms. Clements’ life, propelling her to be-

come a leader in the effort to protect American elementary, middle, and high schools from recurring gun
violence.
Sarah Lerner has been a high school teacher for
25 years. She is a survivor of the Marjory Stoneman
Douglas shooting. On February 14, 2018, she was
teaching her senior English class at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School when the assailant entered
the school and went on his rampage. Ms. Lerner and
15 students hid in her classroom for three hours until
a SWAT team came and let them out. They and other
survivors were then shuttled to a nearby hotel that
served as an informal reunification point for students,
staff, and families.
In Ms. Lerner’s experience, there were no active
shooter drills at Marjory Stoneman Douglas before
the shooting. Since the shooting, the school ha s conducted regular active shooter drills, sometimes several times per year. During the drills, teachers and
students take refuge in designated spaces in their
classrooms, classroom door windows are covered, the
lights are turned off, and everyone tries to stay quiet.
In the years immediately following the shooting,
Ms. Lerner observed that the active shooter drills at
Marjory Stoneman Douglas were highly traumatic because so many of the students had been at the school
during the shooting. Many students cried or even had
full-blown panic attacks during the drills, because the
drills made them relive the events of that day. In
more recent years, there is still trauma from the
drills, but it is of a different kind. This is the generation for whom school shootings in the United States

19
are no longer an extraordinary occurrence. The active
shooter drills further condition the students to accept
the possibility of a shooting at their school, because
shootings at American schools have become a fact of
life. Marjory Stoneman Douglas typically gives parents and students no advance warning of an active
shooter drill, and many parents who get wind that a
drill might occur on a given day will keep their children home that day to protect them from having to
undergo the experience.
Along with Ms. Clements, Ms. Lerner is a cofounder of Teachers Unify to End Gun Violence. M s.
Lerner is angry that such a group needs to exist. She
finds it exasperating that the onus is on teachers, who
are already overburdened, to take the lead to protect
against gun violence in our nation’s schools, while society at large continues to make it so easy for bad actors to target our schoolchildren with what are
essentially weapons of war.5

B. The experience of school nurses and
school psychologists further confirms
the point.
1. School nurses too are on the front lines of safety
in schools. Today, school nurses must deal not just
with scrapes and bruises, fevers, and more serious
physical ailments and injuries, but also with myriad
mental health challenges faced by America’s children
and teenagers. Following an active shooter drill,
school nurses are often “key providers of medical care,
addressing physical symptoms of anxiety or distress—such as panic attacks, hyperventilation, or
psychosomatic symptoms—and working in coordination with [school] mental health staff to provide holistic care.” National Academies, supra , at 245. School
nurses’ experiences regarding active shooter drills are
akin to the experiences of teachers.

21
Cherri Rogers is a school nurse in a public elementary school in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. She has
a doctorate in education and has been in the nursing
profession for more than 30 years.  Her school conducts active shooter drills once a year. Ms. Rogers
says it’s the worst day of the year because she and
other staff members remember Columbine and all the
other school shootings and are reminded that their
school could be next. Because the children at her
school are so young, teachers do not use the term “active shooter drill” with them and instead tell them
more generally that the drills are meant to help everyone practice what they would do in an emergency.
Parents, though, are given advance notice that there
will be an active shooter drill, so that they can opt
their children out if that is their preference. P arents
regularly exercise that option because they understand that the drills, involving a total lockdown of the
school and classrooms, will be frightening and highly
disturbing for their children.
Ms. Rogers explains that if a child is sick and in
the nurse’s room when an active shooter drill begins,
the child stays there and shelters in place with the
nurse for the duration of th e drill. In one such incident, an autistic child was in Ms. Rogers’ room when
an active shooter drill was announced. As the drill got
underway, the child became increasingly fear ful and
anxious, and started shaking. Seeking to comfort him,
Ms. Rogers told him he did not need to worry because
she would do anything to help keep him safe.  She
showed him an iron bar she keeps to shatter the window if evacuation became necessary. Looking back on
that moment, she reflects, “I would take a bullet for a
child. I would. But I shouldn’t have to.”

22
Ms. Rogers is currently running for a seat in the
Pennsylvania state legislature. She supports the Second Amendment, and she and her husband own guns.
But Ms. Rogers’ platform advocates passage of reasonable gun violence prevention measures, reflecting
her life’s work caring for children and others.
Victoria Lyons has been a registered nurse for
more than 30 years. She currently serves as a school
nurse in a public elementary school in Meriden, Connecticut. The school conducts lockdown drills at least
three times per year. The drills are intended to rehearse what to do if intruders, including armed intruders, enter the school.  The drills are not
announced beforehand , so the children, teachers,
staff, and parents do not know when a drill is imminent.
When a drill is announced, Ms. Lyons locks the
door and turns her walkie-talkie down. Ms. Lyons and
any children who happen to be with her in the nurse’s
room go to the designated treatment area in the room
and stay there until they receive the all-clear instruction. Ms. Lyons does her best to comfort the children.
Ms. Lyons tells the children to be quiet, but it is hard
to explain why without saying “because there might
be someone with a gun who wants to shoot us.”
Ms. Lyons finds her school’s lockdown drills futile
and nerve-wracking. Having directly participated in
the drills, s he does not perceive that  the drilling is
likely to enhance the safety of the school’s children
and staff if an active shooter event were actually to
materialize. In her experience, the drills serve chiefly

23
to normalize the ever-present threat of a school shooting, and to suggest to the children that the constant
existence of this threat is just how life is now.
2. “School mental health professionals,” including
school psychologists,  may be “trained to recognize
common trauma reactions .” NASP, supra, at 3. D uring an active shooter drill, they can try to “monitor
participants and remove anyone exhibiting signs of
traumatic stress .” Id. A fter a drill, school psychologists, counselors, and /or social workers will often
meet with students, especially those with a history of
trauma, to “help them navigate the experience.” National Academies, supra, at 303.
Rebecca Norton was a psychologist for 2 8 years,
has a master’s degree in education, and worked as a
school psychologist at a public middle school in
Carpinteria, California, for several years until her retirement in 2022. In her role as a school psychologist,
she supported and counseled middle-schoolers with
intellectual and emotional disabilities.
Ms. Norton’s school conducted regular lockdown
drills, which were intended to address various
threats, including natural disasters like earthquakes,
and also armed intruders on campus. Some of the
drills were pre- announced, but some were not . If a
drill was not pre-announced and a student was in Ms.
Norton’s office when the drill started, the student
would remain with her during the drill. She would
turn the lights off, double -check that the door was
locked (it was supposed to be locked all the time), and
tell any students with her to stay quiet until the drill
was over. Students who were in her office tended to

24
have disabilities of one kind or another. The drills
would typically cause them anxiety and distress, and
Ms. Norton tried to set them at ease.
In Ms. Norton’s experience, the lockdown drills at
her school did not properly take into account the
needs of students who had past trauma or past exposure to violence. More generally, repeated exposure
through drilling to the possibility of school violence
caused distress and fear for both children and staff ,
thereby undermining the efficacy of the learning process. Repeated drilling also had the insidious effect of
habituating students and teachers to the threat of
school shootings and treating the possib ility of a
school shooting as routine.
Ms. Norton explains that she fully appreciates the
importance of protecting students from physical
harm. But she emphasizes that psychological safety is
also essential to a healthy learning environment. In
her experience, persistent reminders of potential violence come at a psychological cost.
“In addition to teachers, school-based health professionals—including school counselors, school psychologists, school social workers, and school
nurses— … play an important role” in “providing ongoing support for the well-being of students and staff.”
National Academies, supra, at 244.  Like the experiences of individual teachers, the experiences of  individual school nurses and school psychologists like Ms.
Rogers, Ms. Lyons, and Ms. Norton  underscore what
underlying research increasingly reveals: School gun
violence, frequently perpetrated with assault weapons, imposes harm not just via the violence itself, but

25
also because active shooter drills, instituted in  response to the violence, undermin e even further our
schoolchildren’s sense of safety, stability, and well-being. Active shooter drills in schools and their baleful
effects are of course just one of the ways that assault
weapons have altered basic aspects of American life,
like the sense of safety in school, that we all used to
take for granted.
CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons and those stated by Respondents, the Court should affirm the decisions below.
